research.query: Fire safety in a Mars habitat
research.answer:
The question was matched to: fire safety, mars. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.
No retrieved passage reports measurements made on Mars itself: what follows are bounds from orbit and Earth, and assumed habitat envelopes.

**Evidence**
- Atmosphere — Mars surface habitat. 26.0–35.0 % O2, 54.0–72.5 kPa, martian (hypothetical). ACME CFI-G: 6 tests inside this envelope; FLEX: 17 tests inside this envelope. [S10]
- SLICE: 3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety. [S1]
- SAFFIRE-I: SAFFIRE-I Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I. Spacecraft Fire, Smoke Distribution. Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus [S2]
- SAFFIRE-III: SAFFIRE-III Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III. Spacecraft Fire Safety. Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus [S3]
- BASS: BASS Burning and Suppression of Solids. Spacecraft Fire Safety. Microgravity Science Glovebox [S4]
- SAME: SAME Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment. Spacecraft Fire Safety. Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware [S5]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S11]
- More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or dr [S12]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.
warnings: Partial gravity: the PSI corpus holds microgravity and 1-g data only — values are bounds, not lunar or martian measurements.

sources.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography — researchImpacts
sources.text: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios.

sources.title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment — researchImpacts
sources.text: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

sources.text: Atmosphere — Mars surface habitat. 26.0–35.0 % O2, 54.0–72.5 kPa, martian (hypothetical). ACME CFI-G: 6 tests inside this envelope; FLEX: 17 tests inside this envelope.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

sources.title: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative
sources.text: Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Limitation: Specific materials and geometries; flow and O2 per test partly only in raw files for BASS.

sources.title: FLEX compares CO2 and helium as gaseous suppressants
sources.text: At 21 % O2, share of FLEX tests ending in flame extinction before burnout by atmosphere — N2 only: 14/29; CO2: 13/18; He: 7/7. FLEX varied CO2 up to 0.7 and He up to 0.45 mole fraction. Limitation: Small samples per cell; droplet size and pressure also vary — use the Extract module to control for them.

top_passage.text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

top_passage.text: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results.

top_passage.text: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.
